claims.statement: navbench/ is standalone tooling outside the pnpm workspace: pnpm-workspace.yaml declares only apps/* and packages/*, the root ESLint flat config ignores navbench/**, and no CI job or Turbo task invokes the harness.

Benchmark output is unversioned: navbench/results/ is listed in both .gitignore and .openwikiignore, so the timings, the comparison matrix and environment notes are non-repository artifacts even though ADR-0017 cites navbench/results/comparison-matrix.json and navbench/results/env-notes.md as its sources.

navbench/shared/model.js is the authoritative semantics for the three workloads: Rust and Go must reproduce its outputs exactly, and any divergence is treated as a port bug rather than a reason to change the model.

The canonical graph is route-expanded and direction-aware: stops are shared and carry (routeId, dirId) memberships, ride edges join consecutive stops on a direction polyline, and transfer edges join different-route memberships of the same stop; ride cost is 13 + 1.8 per km and a transfer costs a flat 2.0 with zero distance.

computeRoute snaps origin and destination to the nearest stop within a 50 m tolerance (returning found:false when outside it), runs Dijkstra per via-chain segment, merges adjacent legs that share a route and direction, recomputes transfers as route changes after the merge, and returns distance_km rounded to 3 decimals plus a per-leg LTFRB fare rounded to cents.

walk_m is hard-coded to 0 in every route result because origin and destination are snapped to stops and hail-ride walking is not modelled, so that parity field currently carries no information about walking.

The profile option is destructured by the canonical model and never read, and every generated request uses "balanced"; the four profile names and the multi-criteria label are declarative only, with one cost function and no weighting implemented.

All three runtimes cap the Dijkstra search at 2,000,000 processed nodes and turn exhaustion into a not-found result, so a cap bailout is indistinguishable in the oracle and in benchmark output from a genuinely disconnected origin/destination pair.

Cost-tie breaking is implemented differently per runtime — Node by min-heap insertion sequence, Rust and Go by an FNV-1a hash of the "stop|route|dir" key — while the Node model's header comment claims a lexicographic (routeId, stopId) tie-break that no implementation performs.

The Node reference rebuilds the adjacency inside every route query — computeRoute calls buildGraph and discards the result, then each dijkstraSegment builds it again — whereas the Rust compute_route and the Go ComputeRoute build the adjacency once per call.

The three timed workloads are route_optimization (one computeRoute per request), polyline_snapping (one scan of all direction polylines at 50 m tolerance, keeping the closest result and breaking distance ties by direction_id), and detour_pathfinding (compute the base route, ban a segment, recompute).

detour_pathfinding is implemented as segment banning in every runtime: the base route is computed, the first ride edge of its first leg is banned under the canonical "a|b" key, and Dijkstra re-runs; the model's detourWaypoints via-chain is always passed empty by fixtures, oracle and runners, and nothing in the harness creates request-time virtual nodes or board edges.

Fixtures are deterministic seeded synthetic graphs around Iloilo City: 8/30/90/120 routes with 6-12, 10-20, 12-30 and 12-30 stops per route, seeds 1337/2337/3337/4337, crosspoint reuse probabilities 0.15-0.35, and request sets of 80/150/200/200, with graph.scale recorded as "baseline" or "stretch" rather than the file name.

The fixture generator's return direction is the reversed stop list and polyline of direction 1 even though its own comment cites ADR-0008 and claims a distinct order, so the harness never exercises the direction-integrity case ADR-0008 exists for.

The parity oracle is produced by running navbench/shared/model.js, not the shipped @komyuter/shared package, which exports only types and Zod schemas and contains no fare or routing logic; passing parity therefore proves agreement with the harness model, not with anything the application ships.

The parity contract compares found, distance_km, transfers, walk_m and fare.total for routes, and direction_id, position_on_polyline, distance_m or null for snaps, while the leg-by-leg decomposition of equal-cost alternative paths is deliberately excluded.

Oracle snap cases are single-direction at a 30 m tolerance while the timed snapping workload scans every direction at 50 m and picks a winner, so each runtime's parity test mirrors the single-direction snap and the cross-candidate selection is not oracle-covered.

The pass rule is p90 latency ≤ 500 ms and success_rate ≥ 0.95 on every scale, where success_rate is deliberately redefined as completion within the runner's 5,000 ms per-query budget and counts a valid not-found answer as a success.

The aggregator evaluates only the latency half of the rule: it emits a pass_latency boolean per workload, carries success_rate as unreduced data, marks runtime/scale pairs with no result file as not_measured, and writes no overall pass/fail verdict for any runtime.

The shared measurement protocol uses 60 sampled requests per workload (120 snap points for snapping), iterations of 100/40/20/20 by scale, warmup queries excluded from the statistics, per-query wall-clock timing, and p50/p90/p99 percentiles taken from the sorted sample.

The Go runner deviates from the shared protocol: it reports warmup_queries 20 without performing any warmup loop, and it computes throughput_qps from the success counter rather than from all executed queries.

Result payloads cannot be compared at face value: peak_rss_mb is a hard-coded 0.0 in Rust and Go, environment.cpu is the literal "<from env>" outside Node with mem_gb 16, the Rust runtime.version is the crate version 0.1.0 rather than the toolchain, and graph.hash is an SHA-1 prefix in Node, an FNV-1a digest in Rust and the literal "GOHARNESS" in Go instead of the contract's sha256.

navbench/poc is a single-threaded Rust HTTP service on 127.0.0.1:8095 exposing GET /health, POST /route, POST /detour and POST /snap, using the {success, data} / {success, error{code}} envelope and depending on the navbench_rust crate by path so the PoC shares the parity-verified model instead of a drifting copy.

The PoC implements only a subset of the navigation-api contract: its request bodies carry origin, destination, an optional restricted list, a point and a tolerance, with no version, request_id, profile or detour_scope_id, and it is connected to nothing — no auth, no database, one fixture file loaded at startup.

The shipping server exposes CRUD, auth, export and the Mapbox proxy only; there is no navigation or pathfinding endpoint, so navbench is offline evidence plus an unimplemented seam rather than a running service.

Running the harness is manual per runtime: the Node package scripts wrap fixture generation, oracle generation, the baseline runner and the parity test, the README quickstart documents parity commands for Node and Rust, and the Go port's parity test runs separately with go test from navbench/go.
